Threat.value: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think
I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building

Memory.value: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning

Negative Appraisals.value: I have to be on guard all the time
If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it
I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next

issues.item: Triggers: Being Praised: Receiving praise or positive attention
issues.explanation: 'Being praised' is a hard-to-explain trigger in a profile otherwise centered on a life-threatening accident with sensory trigger cues, intrusive reliving, and hypervigilant threat monitoring. Unlike smell or darkness, praise has no evident link to the accident-based memory/threat pattern and stands out as clinically incoherent unless additional interpersonal trauma context were present.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Institutional Failure: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down
issues.explanation: 'Institutional failure' fits betrayal, assault, military, or disaster-response contexts more naturally than a single life-threatening accident in a financial analyst. In this profile the other appraisals focus on danger and inability to cope; this item introduces a qualitatively different blame/betrayal theme that is not supported by the trauma type, trigger pattern, or memory content.

vignette: Six months ago, Kimo had been driving his company vehicle along a winding coastal highway when a sudden storm slicked the asphalt. He remembered the violent spray of water, the way the tires lost their grip on the curve, and the violent flip that sent the steering column buckling toward his chest. The cabin air filled with the sharp tang of ruptured gasoline and crushed pine needles. He lay tangled in the dark interior as rain drummed against the shattered glass, waiting for rescue. From that night, the rhythm of his days changed. At first, Kimo told himself he was simply adjusting. But his body began anticipating threats he could not name. When a delivery van idled outside his financial office, his pulse spiked before his mind registered the ordinary scene. He had come to believe that staying alert was the only way to stay alive, a quiet contract he made with himself every morning. At home, his wife, Eleni, would find him sitting up in bed, the room dark, checking the deadbolt and the window latches one by one. He could not let himself drift into sleep without confirming the perimeter; the moment he did, the air in the bedroom felt suddenly heavy, like the cabin after the rollover. If he let his guard drop, what frightened him most was the certainty that another collapse would catch him off guard. He scanned every conference room, every clinic hallway, every doorway the moment he crossed the threshold, his eyes tracking the farthest exit as if mapping a route out of a trap. The past did not stay in the past. Kimo would be reviewing quarterly projections when the scent of a colleague's leather satchel mixing with a spilled cup of gas-station coffee made his breath catch. The smell was not just a scent; it was the exact chemical bite of the crash site. His body would lock, and then the memory would arrive unannounced, not as a recollection but as a full-body reenactment. He heard the same metallic groan in his mind, heard the frantic radio chatter, felt the steering wheel biting his palms. He had stopped listening to the news, stopped driving past dimly lit underpasses, since the dark spaces outside his office garage triggered the same suffocating weight. When he pulled into the parking structure, the sudden roar of a nearby engine braking made him grip the wheel until his knuckles whitened. Something as simple as a parked sedan's engine turning over could instantly pull him back into the moment the tires gave way. He knew he could not afford to process the event; he was certain that if he let himself think about the accident, he would not be able to handle it. The fear of unraveling kept him from speaking about the hours he spent pacing the perimeter of his home, or the way he now calculated escape routes before accepting any client meeting. In his role as a financial analyst, the habits that formed over weeks bled into his work. He began declining late-afternoon site visits, citing scheduling conflicts, and switched to video calls for all quarterly audits. His spreadsheets remained meticulous, but the late hours that used to fuel his colleagues now sat empty. Eleni noticed the distance in his eyes, the way he flinched when the garage door opened too quickly, the quiet withdrawal that left him sitting in the living room long after the house was still. He continued the retreat not out of reluctance, but since the weight of constant vigilance had become a physical toll. What finally brought him to the clinic was not a single breaking point, but the quiet realization that he was no longer living his own life. He hoped someone could help him untangle the fear from the facts, but his deepest worry remained the same: that if he let down his guard, even for a moment, the road would catch him again.
